clinicalPearls: Anejaculation is the complete absence of antegrade ejaculate, which may occur with or without preserved orgasmic sensation
It must be separated from retrograde ejaculation, so a post-orgasmic urine sample is examined; the absence of sperm there indicates true failure of emission rather than backward flow
Causes span neurological injury (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, diabetic autonomic neuropathy), pelvic and retroperitoneal surgery, medications, and psychogenic factors
A situational pattern, with normal nocturnal emissions or ejaculation in some circumstances, points towards a psychogenic rather than organic cause
In spinal cord injury and other neurogenic cases, penile vibratory stimulation and, if unsuccessful, electroejaculation can induce emission for fertility purposes
When induced ejaculation fails or is unsuitable, surgical sperm retrieval from the epididymis or testis provides sperm for intracytoplasmic sperm injection
A careful drug history is essential, as antidepressants, antipsychotics, and sympatholytic agents can impair or abolish ejaculation
reference.pathophysiology: Ejaculation is a two-phase spinal reflex: sympathetic-driven emission deposits sperm and seminal fluid into the posterior urethra with simultaneous bladder-neck closure, followed by rhythmic somatic contraction of the pelvic-floor muscles that expels semen. Anejaculation results when the emission phase fails, so no seminal fluid reaches the urethra. This occurs with interruption of the sympathetic outflow through spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, or retroperitoneal surgery that damages the sympathetic chain, and with drugs that block sympathetic transmission. Psychogenic anejaculation reflects central inhibition of the reflex with an intact peripheral apparatus. Unlike retrograde ejaculation, in which emission occurs but is misdirected into the bladder, true anejaculation produces no semen in either the antegrade ejaculate or the post-orgasmic urine.
additionalDifferentials: Retrograde ejaculation with backward flow of semen
Spinal cord injury or neurological disease
Medication effect, particularly antidepressants and antipsychotics
additionalInvestigations: Post-orgasmic urine analysis to distinguish failure of emission from retrograde ejaculation
Detailed neurological, surgical, and drug history
Blood glucose or HbA1c to detect diabetes
Serum testosterone and gonadotropins to assess the endocrine axis
Scrotal and transrectal ultrasound where obstruction or structural abnormality is suspected
Assessment of nocturnal or situational ejaculation to gauge a psychogenic component
redFlags: New neurological symptoms suggesting spinal cord disease or demyelination
History of recent retroperitoneal or pelvic surgery with autonomic disturbance
Sudden loss of ejaculation with other autonomic features
Associated erectile failure and sensory loss indicating a broader neurological deficit
reference.prognosis: General health is unaffected, and fertility can frequently be achieved using vibratory stimulation, electroejaculation, or surgical sperm retrieval combined with assisted reproduction; psychogenic cases may respond to behavioural or psychological treatment.
pitfalls: Failing to examine post-orgasmic urine and thereby confusing anejaculation with retrograde ejaculation
Overlooking a causative medication that could be modified
Missing an underlying neurological disorder presenting with ejaculatory failure
Assuming an organic cause when the pattern is situational and psychogenic
Delaying referral for assisted reproductive techniques when natural conception is not feasible
references: European Association of Urology guidelines on sexual and reproductive health
WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen
management: Address reversible causes by reviewing and modifying offending sympatholytic medications and optimising glycaemic control in diabetic autonomic neuropathy
Penile vibratory stimulation as first-line to induce emission in neurogenic anejaculation such as spinal cord injury
Electroejaculation under specialist supervision when vibratory stimulation fails
Surgical sperm retrieval from the epididymis or testis for intracytoplasmic sperm injection when induced ejaculation is unsuccessful or unsuitable
Psychosexual therapy and behavioural treatment for situational or psychogenic anejaculation
Autonomic dysreflexia precautions with blood-pressure monitoring during vibratory or electroejaculation in high-level spinal cord injury
Referral to andrology and assisted reproduction services for fertility planning
